questions.question: Explain how indigenous healing understands the physical and spiritual causes of illness.
questions.expected_answer: Indigenous healing recognises physical causes such as injuries, burns and broken bones, spoiled food, dirty water, insect bites, snakebites, cold, infections and old age, treated with plant medicines, ointments, steaming and setting bones. Many people also believe some illnesses have spiritual causes, for example if customs are neglected or the ancestors are not honoured, or the ill will of others. So healing looks at the whole person: body, mind, family, community and ancestors in balance.

questions.question: Describe the roles of herbalists and diviners.
questions.expected_answer: Herbalists, called inyanga in isiZulu and ixhwele in isiXhosa, are experts in medicines made from plants, roots and bark, knowing which treat which illnesses and how to prepare them. Diviners, called isangoma in isiZulu and igqirha in isiXhosa, are believed to communicate with the ancestors to find the cause of a problem. Many say they were called by the ancestors and trained for a long time; they may throw bones or interpret dreams and lead ceremonies, singing and drumming.

questions.question: Describe the place of indigenous healing in South Africa today.
questions.expected_answer: Many South Africans consult traditional healers, and many use both traditional healers and clinics. Traditional healing was looked down on and restricted under colonialism and apartheid, but the Traditional Health Practitioners Act of 2007 recognises healers and set up a council to register them and set standards. In some areas, healers are trained to recognise TB and HIV and refer patients to clinics. There are concerns about harmful doses and delays in treatment, so cooperation matters.
